summary: Defines an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that tells transit routers to look more closely at a packet instead of just forwarding it. It is used by protocols that need routers along the path to inspect certain messages. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a sticker on a package saying every post office on the way should open this one and read it.

questions: what is the ipv6 router alert option
how do routers inspect special ipv6 packets
what are the router alert option values

subtitle: A Hop-by-Hop option that tells IPv6 routers a packet deserves a closer look.

tldr.problem: Routers had to partly parse upper-layer data in every datagram to find the few that carry control messages like RSVP, which is expensive and slow.
tldr.mechanism: A new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option, the Router Alert, flags a datagram as interesting to routers, whose value field says what kind of message it carries.
tldr.outcome: Normal datagrams are forwarded with little or no penalty. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 6398 and RFC 9805.

today: RFC 2711 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6398 and RFC 9805.

sections.title: Why Routers Need an Alert
sections.content:
Protocols such as RSVP use control datagrams that are addressed to a particular destination but need to be examined, and sometimes updated, by routers along the path. Until now, the only way for a router to know it needed to look was to at least partially parse upper-layer data in all datagrams, which is expensive and slow.

The RFC adds an option inside the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop header. Its presence tells the router the datagram is of interest. Its absence tells the router the datagram can safely be routed without further parsing. Hosts originating IPv6 datagrams are required to include it in certain circumstances.
sections.plainLanguage: Without the sticker, the post office would have to peek inside every parcel. With it, only the marked ones get opened.

sections.title: The Approach
sections.content:
The goal is an efficient mechanism so routers know when to intercept datagrams not addressed to them without extensively examining every datagram. The solution is a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option meaning that routers should examine this datagram more closely, with protocols such as RSVP required to use it.

This approach incurs little or no performance penalty on forwarding normal datagrams, because not including the option tells the router there is no need to closely examine the contents.
sections.plainLanguage: Mark only the special parcels, and the post office does not slow down for the rest.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The option has a type, a length of 2 and a 2-octet value. The first three bits of the type octet are zero and the remaining five bits hold the Hop-by-Hop Option Type number 5. Zeroing the first three bits means a node that does not recognize the option skips over it and continues processing, and that the option must not change en route. There MUST be only one such option per Hop-by-Hop header. The alignment requirement is 2n+0.

The value, in network byte order, is 0 for a Multicast Listener Discovery message, 1 for an RSVP message and 2 for an Active Networks message. Values 3 to 65535 are reserved to IANA for future use.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker has a small code on it that says what is inside: a group-joining note, a reservation request, or something else.

sections.title: How Nodes Treat the Option
sections.content:
The option says the contents may be interesting to the router. What the router does is specified in the RFC of the protocol that mandates or allows the option. Routers that recognize it examine the datagram more closely, parsing just enough to decide whether further processing is needed, and the value field can speed this up.

The final destination MUST ignore the option, to prevent multiple evaluations. Unrecognized values MUST be silently ignored and processing continues. If a router must examine the payload, it is performing a host function and SHOULD interpret the data as a host.

For the option to work, its use MUST be mandated in protocols that expect routers to do significant processing on datagrams not addressed to them. All IPv6 datagrams containing an RSVP message MUST contain this option.
sections.plainLanguage: The router reads only enough to decide if the parcel matters. The person it is addressed to ignores the sticker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Gratuitous use of the option can cause performance problems in routers. A more severe attack floods a router with bogus datagrams that carry router alert options. A router that supports the option MAY limit its use by rate or other means.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone sticks the sticker on junk, the post office wastes time opening it, so it may limit how many it opens.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The value field is registered and maintained by IANA. New values are assigned through IETF Consensus as defined in RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: A librarian keeps the official list of sticker codes, and new codes need broad agreement.

fields.name: Action bits
fields.desc: All zero: skip if unrecognized, option does not change en route.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value field in octets.
